title: To Stop Cheating in School, Address the Root Cause roundup, September 6, 2026 adam-grant/
author: Grant, Adam
source: Adam Grant, republished on Larry Cuban's blog, via Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #122
summary: Adam Grant argues that the standard institutional response to AI-enabled cheating -- adding obstacles like redesigned exams and honesty pledges -- treats a symptom rather than the underlying cause, which is that students no longer experience cheating as a moral violation. His diagnosis is that AI has made cheating 'so effortless, enticing and available' that students compartmentalize it: they will admit to sometimes cheating while insisting they are not cheaters, protecting a self-image of integrity even while violating it. His proposed fix is deliberately building students' moral identity -- the disposition to ask 'what's the right thing for someone like me to do' rather than calculating whether an act will get caught -- and he points to ethics education among financial advisers as real-world evidence that this kind of identity-based intervention changes behavior for years afterward, with the effect strongest among the least experienced advisers. The underlying research on honesty pledges that Grant's 'a pledge doubled cheating' claim draws attention to (a large 2024 Nature Human Behaviour study of over 21,000 participants testing 21 pledge wordings) actually found a more complicated picture than a simple failure: most tested wordings modestly improved honesty and the best one nearly halved dishonest behavior, but the effect depended heavily on specific wording, and even expert reviewers were largely unable to predict in advance which wordings would work -- reinforcing Grant's own point that surface-level interventions like a generic pledge are unreliable unless they are built with real understanding of what actually shapes a person's sense of identity and character.
points: Grant's core diagnosis is that AI has made cheating 'so effortless, enticing and available' that many students have stopped experiencing it as a moral violation, allowing them to compartmentalize: 'they'd sometimes cheated, but they weren't cheaters.'

He argues that obstacle-based fixes (redesigned exams, honesty pledges) address symptoms, not the cause, and that the real fix is building students' moral identity -- the habit of asking 'what's the right thing for someone like me to do.'

As real-world evidence, Grant cites ethics education among financial advisers, finding it produced a lasting reduction in professional misconduct, with the strongest effect among the least experienced advisers.

The specific academic research behind pledge-effectiveness claims (Zickfeld, Scigala, Elbaek et al., Nature Human Behaviour, 2024) tested 21 different honesty-pledge wordings on over 21,000 participants and found most modestly improved honesty and the best wording nearly halved evasion -- but success depended heavily on exact wording, and even experts could not reliably predict which wordings would work in advance.

Grant's summary formulation of his own argument is that 'what we achieve may define our success' but 'how we achieve it determines our character,' framing character formation, not enforcement, as the durable solution.
quotes: It's made cheating so effortless, enticing and available that many students no longer believe it's wrong.
The heart of integrity is recognizing that the ends don't justify the means.
Studying ethics was especially influential for advisers who were inexperienced.
What we achieve may define our success. How we achieve it determines our character.

Ten of the 21 pledge wordings significantly improved honest behavior, with compliance gains of 4.5 to 8.5 percentage points, and the most effective wording nearly halved evasion -- but the researchers found the effect depended heavily on the specific wording used, and experts largely failed to predict in advance which wordings would work.
